Our work thus highlights a novel and significant application for internal causal analysis of language models.

papers.title: First Align, then Predict: Understanding the Cross-Lingual Ability of Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: What parts of the model and what mechanisms support zero-shot cross-lingual transfer in multilingual BERT?
papers.core_contribution: mBERT operates as the stacking of two modules: a multilingual encoder in the lower layers critical for cross-lingual transfer, and a task-specific, language-agnostic predictor in the upper layers that has little importance for transfer.
papers.conclusion: mBERT is constructed from a multilingual encoder in the lower layers that aligns representations across languages and is critical for cross-language transfer, and a task-specific, language-agnostic predictor in the upper layers that has little effect on transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Lower layers of mBERT are critical for cross-lingual transfer, while upper layers are task-specific and language-agnostic.
Cross-lingual similarity (CKA) between representations of source and target languages is highest in the middle layers and strongly correlates with cross-lingual performance.
Randomly initializing lower layers harms cross-lingual performance but not same-language performance, indicating their specific role in cross-lingual alignment.
The cross-lingual alignment learned during pretraining is preserved after fine-tuning.
This mechanism suggests mBERT reproduces the standard cross-lingual pipeline without explicit supervision.
future_direction: Using the findings to design better multilingual pre-training processes.
Inspecting the mismatch with Singh et al. (2019) who found no language alignment across layers for Natural Language Inference.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pretrained language models have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot crosslingual transfer capabilities. Such transfer emerges by fine-tuning on a task of interest in one language and evaluating on a distinct language, not seen during the fine-tuning. Despite promising results, we still lack a proper understanding of the source of this transfer. Using a novel layer ablation technique and analyses of the model's internal representations, we show that multilingual BERT, a popular multilingual language model, can be viewed as the stacking of two sub-networks: a multilingual encoder followed by a taskspecific language-agnostic predictor. While the encoder is crucial for cross-lingual transfer and remains mostly unchanged during finetuning, the task predictor has little importance on the transfer and can be reinitialized during fine-tuning. We present extensive experiments with three distinct tasks, seventeen typologically diverse languages and multiple domains to support our hypothesis.

papers.title: Turning the Spell Around: Lightweight Alignment Amplification via Rank-One Safety Injection
papers.research_question: Can we systematically amplify safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RANK-ONE SAFETY INJECTION (ROSI), a fine-tuning-free weight-editing method that amplifies safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward a refusal-mediating subspace.
papers.conclusion: ROSI is a simple, effective, and interpretable method to enhance LLM safety, demonstrating the practical value of mechanistic interpretability for designing efficient safety interventions.
papers.key_findings:
ROSI consistently improves harm refusal rates in aligned models while preserving utility on standard benchmarks.
ROSI makes aligned models more robust to a suite of adversarial jailbreak attacks.
ROSI can inject safety into uncensored models (e.g., DOLPHIN), effectively re-aligning them without retraining.
The safety direction is largely orthogonal to utility representations, allowing safety amplification with minimal side effects.
A safety system prompt is crucial for extracting a meaningful safety direction from uncensored models.
papers.limitation: Smaller models (≤ 1B) show the biggest degradation in benign compliance (BC) when applying ROSI.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated methods for identifying and manipulating conceptual directions
Extending the approach to other desirable model attributes beyond safety, such as honesty or controllability
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) often involves mediating internal representations to refuse harmful requests. Recent research has demonstrated that these safety mechanisms can be bypassed by ablating or removing specific representational directions within the model. In this paper, we propose the opposite approach: Rank-One Safety Injection (ROSI), a white-box method that amplifies a model's safety alignment by permanently steering its activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace. ROSI operates as a simple, fine-tuning-free rank-one weight modification applied to all residual stream write matrices. The required safety direction can be computed from a small set of harmful and harmless instruction pairs. We show that ROSI consistently increases safety refusal rates - as evaluated by Llama Guard 3 - while preserving the utility of the model on standard benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, and Arc. Furthermore, we show that ROSI can also re-align 'uncensored' models by amplifying their own latent safety directions, demonstrating its utility as an effective last-mile safety procedure. Our results suggest that targeted, interpretable weight steering is a cheap and potent mechanism to improve LLM safety, complementing more resource-intensive fine-tuning paradigms.

papers.title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models represent different linguistic phenomena, and are linguistically similar phenomena represented similarly in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method using linguistic minimal pairs to measure linguistic similarity in LLMs, revealing that linguistic similarity is influenced by training data, aligns with fine-grained linguistic categories, weakly correlates with semantic similarity, and shows limited cross-lingual alignment.
papers.conclusion: The work provides insights into LLMs' internal language processing, bridging neural models and linguistic theory, and offers a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages.
Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones.
Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, indicating its context-dependent nature.
LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Dependent on the quality and scope of existing linguistic minimal pair datasets
Limited to three languages, not representing global linguistic diversity
Only captures a fraction of language's complexity with 150 phenomena
future_direction: Developing more high-quality minimal pairs
Broadening language coverage to include more diverse linguistic families
Increasing the range of phenomena studied
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel analysis that leverages linguistic minimal pairs to probe the internal linguistic representations of Large Language Models (LLMs). By measuring the similarity between LLM activation differences across minimal pairs, we quantify the and gain insight into the linguistic knowledge captured by LLMs. Our large-scale experiments, spanning 100+ LLMs and 150k minimal pairs in three languages, reveal properties of linguistic similarity from four key aspects: consistency across LLMs, relation to theoretical categorizations, dependency to semantic context, and cross-lingual alignment of relevant phenomena. Our findings suggest that 1) linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages. 2) Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones. 3) Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, showing its context-dependent nature. 4) LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena. This work demonstrates the potential of minimal pairs as a window into the neural representations of language in LLMs, shedding light on the relationship between LLMs and linguistic theory. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/ChenDelong1999/Linguistic-Similarity

papers.title: Scaling sparse feature circuit finding for in-context learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to understand the mechanism of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify task-detection and task-execution features in the in-context learning circuit of large language models, and introduces the Task Vector Cleaning algorithm to decompose task vectors into interpretable features.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance understanding of in-context learning mechanisms and demonstrate the potential of sparse autoencoders as a powerful tool for interpretability research on larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can be used to analyze in-context learning in larger models like Gemma-1 2B, scaling up circuit analysis.
Task-execution features encode task knowledge and can causally induce task zero-shot performance.
Task-detection features identify tasks from the prompt and are causally linked to execution features via attention and MLP sublayers.
The Task Vector Cleaning algorithm effectively decomposes task vectors into sparse, interpretable features while preserving their effect on loss.
The in-context learning circuit involves interaction between detection and execution features through attention and MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
Circuit search was constrained to intermediate layers due to early layers processing token-level information and having lower quality Indirect Effect approximations.
Hundreds of features needed to be ablated to achieve significant faithfulness degradation, unlike prior work which required fewer.
Negative steering experiments showed lower task specificity, indicating steering experiments alone may not suffice for comprehensive analysis.
future_direction: Improving SAE training to yield more monosemantic features.
Scaling circuit analysis to even larger models.
Applying these techniques to more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular tool for interpreting large language model activations, but their utility in addressing open questions in interpretability remains unclear. In this work, we demonstrate their effectiveness by using SAEs to deepen our understanding of the mechanism behind in-context learning (ICL). We identify abstract SAE features that (i) encode the model's knowledge of which task to execute and (ii) whose latent vectors causally induce the task zero-shot. This aligns with prior work showing that ICL is mediated by task vectors. We further demonstrate that these task vectors are well approximated by a sparse sum of SAE latents, including these task-execution features. To explore the ICL mechanism, we adapt the sparse feature circuits methodology of Marks et al. (2024) to work for the much larger Gemma-1 2B model, with 30 times as many parameters, and to the more complex task of ICL. Through circuit finding, we discover task-detecting features with corresponding SAE latents that activate earlier in the prompt, that detect when tasks have been performed. They are causally linked with task-execution features through the attention and MLP sublayers.

papers.title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphosyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages.
papers.core_contribution: Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.
papers.conclusion: Large language models share representations of morphosyntactic concepts across typologically diverse languages, suggesting that they develop cross-lingual abstractions, even when trained primarily on English.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of morphosyntactic concepts are shared across languages, with significant overlap in the top features encoding grammatical categories.
Probing classifiers crucially rely on multilingual features to predict morphosyntactic concepts; ablating multilingual features drops performance to near-chance.
Intervening on single multilingual features can change model behavior in machine translation tasks, demonstrating their causal role.
Interventions are selective, primarily affecting the targeted concept without interfering with other concepts.
Sparse autoencoder features are human-interpretable and activate on relevant grammatical concepts across languages.
papers.limitation:
Distinction between model understanding and generation; some features with high causal effect on probes do not necessarily affect generation.
Human biases in feature interpretation; human explanations of features may be biased and suboptimal.
Sparse autoencoders only recover linearly encoded features; non-linearly encoded concepts may not be captured.
papers.abstract: Human bilinguals often use similar brain regions to process multiple languages, depending on when they learned their second language and their proficiency. In large language models (LLMs), how are multiple languages learned and encoded? In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphsyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages. We train sparse autoencoders on Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B, and demonstrate that abstract grammatical concepts are often encoded in feature directions shared across many languages. We use causal interventions to verify the multilingual nature of these representations; specifically, we show that ablating only multilingual features decreases classifier performance to near-chance across languages. We then use these features to precisely modify model behavior in a machine translation task; this demonstrates both the generality and selectivity of these feature's roles in the network. Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.

papers.title: Soteria: Language-Specific Functional Parameter Steering for Multilingual Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we ensure consistent safety across multiple languages in large language models by locating and minimally adjusting language-specific functional parameters?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Soteria, a lightweight method that identifies and adjusts language-specific functional attention heads to improve multilingual safety alignment by modifying only ~3% of parameters, reducing harmful outputs without degrading overall model performance.
papers.conclusion: Soteria provides an effective, parameter-efficient path to scalable multilingual safety alignment, enhancing model safety across diverse languages without compromising utility.
papers.key_findings:
Soteria significantly reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) across high-, mid-, and low-resource languages on safety benchmarks like MultiJail and XThreatBench.
The method outperforms baseline safety alignment techniques such as Safety Arithmetic, Resta, and TIES.
Modifying only the O-projection weights of identified functional heads preserves general model capabilities, as shown by stable MMLU scores.
Attention head analysis reveals that high- and mid-resource languages share functional heads in mid-layers, while low-resource languages utilize heads in later layers.
The approach is robust against state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks like POATE and RDR.
papers.limitation:
Relies on per-language functional neuron identification, which requires accurate language segmentation and task-based data in each target language; resource constraints and data limitations can reduce selection precision.
Does not guarantee comprehensive coverage of every cultural nuance or emergent harmful behavior.
future_direction: Investigating attention-head analysis to tackle task-specific heads, misalignment, and hallucination issues.
Enhancing universal attention heads to improve cross-lingual understanding and zero-shot performance for underrepresented languages.
Refining or shifting the latent space of problematic heads to improve overall alignment and trustworthiness.
papers.abstract: Ensuring consistent safety across multiple languages remains a significant challenge for large language models (LLMs). We introduce Soteria, a lightweight yet powerful strategy that locates and minimally adjusts the "functional heads" most responsible for harmful content generation in each language. By altering only a fraction of parameters, Soteria drastically reduces policy violations without sacrificing overall model performance, even in low-resource settings. To rigorously evaluate our approach, we also present XThreatBench, a specialized multilingual dataset capturing fine-grained harmful behaviors drawn from real policy guidelines. Experiments with leading open-source LLMs (e.g., Llama, Qwen, Mistral) show that Soteria consistently improves safety metrics across high-, mid-, and low-resource languages. These findings highlight a promising path toward scalable, linguistically attuned, and ethically aligned LLMs worldwide.

papers.title: Estimating the Causal Effects of Natural Logic Features in Neural NLI Models
papers.research_question: How can we estimate the causal effects of semantic features like context monotonicity and word-pair relations on neural NLI model predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a causal intervention framework to estimate the effects of semantic features on NLI model predictions, enabling comparison of model robustness and sensitivity.
papers.conclusion: Causal effect estimation provides insights into model behavior, showing that benchmark accuracy does not guarantee robustness to semantic features, and fine-tuning on targeted datasets can improve sensitivity.
papers.key_findings:
HELP fine-tuning improves model sensitivity to context changes and robustness to irrelevant word-pair changes.
High-performing models on benchmarks may exhibit poor causal robustness to semantic features.
Models often over-rely on word relations and ignore context monotonicity.
Causal effect measures reveal behavioral differences not captured by benchmark accuracy.
The methodology allows quantifying undesired direct effects and desired total effects.
papers.limitation:
Potential label inconsistencies between models and datasets.
Reliance on prior causal modeling from Stolfo et al. (2022) which may have inconsistencies.
Causal effect estimates are sample-specific and could be improved with larger data.
papers.abstract: Rigorous evaluation of the causal effects of semantic features on language model predictions can be hard to achieve for natural language reasoning problems. However, this is such a desirable form of analysis from both an interpretability and model evaluation perspective, that it is valuable to zone in on specific patterns of reasoning with enough structure and regularity to be able to identify and quantify systematic reasoning failures in widely-used models. In this vein, we pick a portion of the NLI task for which an explicit causal diagram can be systematically constructed: in particular, the case where across two sentences (the premise and hypothesis), two related words/terms occur in a shared context. In this work, we apply causal effect estimation strategies to measure the effect of context interventions (whose effect on the entailment label is mediated by the semantic monotonicity characteristic) and interventions on the inserted word-pair (whose effect on the entailment label is mediated by the relation between these words.). Following related work on causal analysis of NLP models in different settings, we adapt the methodology for the NLI task to construct comparative model profiles in terms of robustness to irrelevant changes and sensitivity to impactful changes.

papers.title: SABER: Uncovering Vulnerabilities in Safety Alignment via Cross-Layer Residual Connection
papers.research_question: How can safety alignment in Large Language Models be bypassed by exploiting the layer-wise distribution of safety mechanisms and using cross-layer residual connections?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SABER, a white-box jailbreak method that uses a cross-layer residual connection to bypass safety alignment in LLMs by routing information around safety-enforcing middle-to-late layers.
papers.conclusion: SABER is an effective jailbreak method that highlights a critical vulnerability in open-source language models to subtle architectural perturbations, demonstrating that safety alignment can be circumvented via cross-layer residual connections.
papers.key_findings:
Safety mechanisms in LLMs are predominantly embedded in the middle-to-late layers.
SABER achieves up to a 51% improvement in Attack Success Rate over the best-performing baseline on the HarmBench test set.
SABER induces only a marginal shift in perplexity on benign inputs, preserving general language capabilities.
Euclidean norm-based scaling is a critical component for SABER's effectiveness.
SABER creates an alternative pathway that reduces denial responses without significantly increasing hallucinations, balancing attack success and output coherence.
papers.limitation: The outcome when more than one layer is connected is still unexplored.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) with safe-alignment training are powerful instruments with robust language comprehension capabilities. These models typically undergo meticulous alignment procedures involving human feedback to ensure the acceptance of safe inputs while rejecting harmful or unsafe ones. However, despite their massive scale and alignment efforts, LLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where malicious users manipulate the model to produce harmful outputs that it was explicitly trained to avoid. In this study, we find that the safety mechanisms in LLMs are predominantly embedded in the middle-to-late layers. Building on this insight, we introduce a novel white-box jailbreak method, SABER (Safety Alignment Bypass via Extra Residuals), which connects two intermediate layers $s$ and $e$ such that $s < e$, through a residual connection. Our approach achieves a 51% improvement over the best-performing baseline on the HarmBench test set. Furthermore, SABER induces only a marginal shift in perplexity when evaluated on the HarmBench validation set. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/PalGitts/SABER.

papers.title: The Geometry of Multilingual Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models maintain a shared representation space while encoding language-sensitive information in each language?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, facilitating feature extraction for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual language models encode features by projecting representations onto orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes in the representation space, enabling efficient extraction for various tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, as shown by perplexity comparisons and subspace distances.
Subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that encode information such as token vocabularies, and shifting representations by language means can induce token predictions in different languages.
There are stable language-neutral axes that encode information like token positions and part-of-speech, which are orthogonal to language-sensitive axes.
Language-sensitive and language-neutral axes are relatively stable across middle layers, with minimal transformation as representations pass through.
Token position information is encoded along nonlinear structures such as spirals and toruses in the representation space.
future_direction: Assess how multilingual language models encode more complex linguistic features geometrically.
Investigate how nonlinear structures like spirals and toruses arise from and interact with the self-attention mechanism.
Conduct a more detailed analysis of how specific representational structures are retained across layers.
papers.abstract: We assess how multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language. Using XLM-R as a case study, we show that languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, evaluated based on causal effects on language modeling performance and direct comparisons between subspaces for 88 languages. The subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that are relatively stable throughout middle layers, and these axes encode information such as token vocabularies. Shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages. However, we also identify stable language-neutral axes that encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech. We visualize representations projected onto language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, identifying language family and part-of-speech clusters, along with spirals, toruses, and curves representing token position information. These results demonstrate that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, allowing the models to extract a variety of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: InversionView: A General-Purpose Method for Reading Information from Neural Activations
papers.research_question: How can we decipher the information encoded in neural activations? The paper proposes InversionView, a method to sample from the preimage of an activation to uncover the information content.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces InversionView, a method that samples from the preimage of an activation via a conditional decoder to uncover the information encoded in neural activations and understand model algorithms.
papers.conclusion: InversionView is a general-purpose method that effectively deciphers information in neural activations, enabling better understanding of model algorithms and simplifying interpretability workflows.
papers.key_findings:
InversionView can reveal both basic and complex information in activations, such as token counts and relative positions.
InversionView simplifies interpretability workflows, agreeing with prior circuit findings in GPT-2 small.
InversionView enabled the first fully verified circuit for a 3-digit addition model.
InversionView scales to larger models like GPT-2 for factual recall.
papers.limitation:
Training a decoder requires a dataset of activations and can be computationally expensive.
The decoder may not perfectly capture the preimage, leading to potential biases in the generated samples.
The method is currently limited to discrete sequences (text).
future_direction: Extend InversionView to continuous domains.
Improve decoder efficiency.
Automate interpretation using LLMs.
papers.abstract: The inner workings of neural networks can be better understood if we can fully decipher the information encoded in neural activations. In this paper, we argue that this information is embodied by the subset of inputs that give rise to similar activations. We propose InversionView, which allows us to practically inspect this subset by sampling from a trained decoder model conditioned on activations. This helps uncover the information content of activation vectors, and facilitates understanding of the algorithms implemented by transformer models. We present four case studies where we investigate models ranging from small transformers to GPT-2. In these studies, we show that InversionView can reveal clear information contained in activations, including basic information about tokens appearing in the context, as well as more complex information, such as the count of certain tokens, their relative positions, and abstract knowledge about the subject. We also provide causally verified circuits to confirm the decoded information.

papers.title: Neural Natural Language Inference Models Partially Embed Theories of Lexical Entailment and Negation
papers.research_question: Whether neural models for Natural Language Inference (NLI) can learn the compositional interactions between lexical entailment and negation.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a BERT-based model, after fine-tuning, can learn to reason about lexical entailment and negation, and structural evaluations (probes and interventions) provide evidence that the model partially embeds the target monotonicity algorithm.
papers.conclusion: The BERT model at least partially embeds a theory of lexical entailment and negation at an algorithmic level, in addition to achieving the correct input-output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on general-purpose NLI datasets (SNLI/MNLI) fail systematically on examples requiring negation to reverse lexical entailment.
Fine-tuning on a subset of the MoNLI dataset enables models to solve a systematic generalization task requiring lexical entailment and negation.
Probing experiments show that BERT's internal representations correlate with the lexical entailment relation and the algorithm's output.
Interchange intervention experiments show that BERT's causal dynamics mirror the monotonicity algorithm on specific subsets of the MoNLI data.
papers.limitation:
The interchange intervention methodology is not yet formally grounded.
The analysis only shows that BERT mimics the algorithm on subsets of MoNLI, not on the entire dataset.
papers.abstract: We address whether neural models for Natural Language Inference (NLI) can learn the compositional interactions between lexical entailment and negation, using four methods: the behavioral evaluation methods of (1) challenge test sets and (2) systematic generalization tasks, and the structural evaluation methods of (3) probes and (4) interventions. To facilitate this holistic evaluation, we present Monotonicity NLI (MoNLI), a new naturalistic dataset focused on lexical entailment and negation. In our behavioral evaluations, we find that models trained on general-purpose NLI datasets fail systematically on MoNLI examples containing negation, but that MoNLI fine-tuning addresses this failure. In our structural evaluations, we look for evidence that our top-performing BERT-based model has learned to implement the monotonicity algorithm behind MoNLI. Probes yield evidence consistent with this conclusion, and our intervention experiments bolster this, showing that the causal dynamics of the model mirror the causal dynamics of this algorithm on subsets of MoNLI. This suggests that the BERT model at least partially embeds a theory of lexical entailment and negation at an algorithmic level.

papers.title: Estimating the Causal Effects of Natural Logic Features in Transformer-Based NLI Models
papers.research_question: How can we estimate the causal effects of semantic features (context monotonicity and word-pair relations) on transformer-based NLI model predictions, and what does this reveal about model robustness and sensitivity?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a causal effect estimation framework for analyzing NLI models, measuring their sensitivity to relevant semantic feature changes and robustness to irrelevant ones. It shows that benchmark accuracy does not reflect these properties and that fine-tuning on a targeted dataset (HELP) can improve both robustness and sensitivity.
papers.conclusion: Causal effect estimation provides a granular view of model behavior, revealing biases and robustness issues not captured by benchmark accuracy, and demonstrates that targeted interventions can improve model reasoning properties.
papers.key_findings:
Models with similar benchmark accuracy can exhibit very different behavior in terms of sensitivity and robustness to semantic features.
Models fine-tuned on the HELP dataset show improved robustness to irrelevant word-pair changes and sensitivity to relevant context changes.
Large models like roberta-large-mnli exhibit poor context sensitivity, indicating a bias towards upward-monotone contexts and ignoring negation markers.
Causal effect measures reveal that even high-performing models can systematically fail to adapt predictions to changing context structure, suggesting over-reliance on word relations.
Strategies to improve responsiveness to context changes (e.g., HELP fine-tuning) also increase robustness to irrelevant word-pair changes.
papers.abstract: Rigorous evaluation of the causal effects of semantic features on language model predictions can be hard to achieve for natural language reasoning problems. However, this is such a desirable form of analysis from both an interpretability and model evaluation perspective, that it is valuable to investigate specific patterns of reasoning with enough structure and regularity to identify and quantify systematic reasoning failures in widely-used models. In this vein, we pick a portion of the NLI task for which an explicit causal diagram can be systematically constructed: the case where across two sentences (the premise and hypothesis), two related words/terms occur in a shared context. In this work, we apply causal effect estimation strategies to measure the effect of context interventions (whose effect on the entailment label is mediated by the semantic monotonicity characteristic) and interventions on the inserted word-pair (whose effect on the entailment label is mediated by the relation between these words). Extending related work on causal analysis of NLP models in different settings, we perform an extensive interventional study on the NLI task to investigate robustness to irrelevant changes and sensitivity to impactful changes of Transformers. The results strongly bolster the fact that similar benchmark accuracy scores may be observed for models that exhibit very different behaviour. Moreover, our methodology reinforces previously suspected biases from a causal perspective, including biases in favour of upward-monotone contexts and ignoring the effects of negation markers.

papers.title: Large Language Models are In-Context Semantic Reasoners rather than Symbolic Reasoners
papers.research_question: Are LLMs good in-context reasoners without semantics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that semantics are vital for LLMs' in-context reasoning; they perform well when semantics align with commonsense but struggle with symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning, relying on superficial semantic connections rather than formal symbolic reasoning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs rely heavily on learned semantics for in-context reasoning, creating strong token connections that compose a superficial logical chain, rather than performing formal symbolic reasoning like humans.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform significantly better on reasoning tasks when semantics are consistent with commonsense compared to when semantics are decoupled (symbolic setting).
LLMs struggle to solve symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning tasks by leveraging in-context new knowledge.
Semantic knowledge is easier for LLMs to memorize than symbolic knowledge, but updating semantic knowledge has a higher forgetting ratio due to stronger correlations.
LLMs' reasoning performance is inferior to logic-based symbolic methods across all tested reasoning tasks (deduction, induction, abduction).
The length of the in-context information impacts reasoning performance, with shorter contexts leading to better results.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to specific datasets (Symbolic Tree, ProofWriter) and models (ChatGPT, GPT-4, LLaMA-7B).
Long-context reasoning is challenging for LLMs, as they struggle to select relevant information from excessively long prompts.
future_direction: Combining LLMs with non-parametric knowledge bases (e.g., graph databases) for more efficient and accurate knowledge updating and reasoning.
Further research on neural-symbolic AI systems to leverage the strengths of both neural and symbolic approaches.
Investigating the internal mechanisms of LLMs to better understand how they utilize semantics for reasoning.
papers.abstract: The emergent few-shot reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have excited the natural language and machine learning community over recent years. Despite of numerous successful applications, the underlying mechanism of such in-context capabilities still remains unclear. In this work, we hypothesize that the learned \textit{semantics} of language tokens do the most heavy lifting during the reasoning process. Different from human's symbolic reasoning process, the semantic representations of LLMs could create strong connections among tokens, thus composing a superficial logical chain. To test our hypothesis, we decouple semantics from the language reasoning process and evaluate three kinds of reasoning abilities, i.e., deduction, induction and abduction. Our findings reveal that semantics play a vital role in LLMs' in-context reasoning -- LLMs perform significantly better when semantics are consistent with commonsense but struggle to solve symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning tasks by leveraging in-context new knowledge. The surprising observations question whether modern LLMs have mastered the inductive, deductive and abductive reasoning abilities as in human intelligence, and motivate research on unveiling the magic existing within the black-box LLMs. On the whole, our analysis provides a novel perspective on the role of semantics in developing and evaluating language models' reasoning abilities. Code is available at {\url{https://github.com/XiaojuanTang/ICSR}}.

papers.title: LLaVA Steering: Visual Instruction Tuning with 500x Fewer Parameters through Modality Linear Representation-Steering
papers.research_question: How can the number of trainable parameters for visual instruction tuning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be significantly reduced by addressing the intrinsic imbalance between text and visual modalities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Modality Linear Representation-Steering (MoReS), a method that rebalances text and visual modalities in MLLMs by steering visual representations through linear transformations, achieving comparable performance to LoRA with 500x fewer trainable parameters.
papers.conclusion: MoReS provides an efficient and effective approach for visual instruction tuning in MLLMs by addressing modality imbalance, significantly reducing parameter count while maintaining performance, and offering a pathway for more accessible and customizable multimodal model development.
papers.key_findings:
MoReS requires 287 to 1,150 times fewer trainable parameters than LoRA while maintaining competitive performance on multiple visual benchmarks.
MoReS effectively rebalances the attention distribution between visual and textual representations, mitigating the intrinsic modality imbalance in MLLMs.
The method reduces hallucination in MLLMs, as shown by improved performance on POPE and HallucinationBench.
MoReS preserves the LLM's pre-trained world knowledge and performs well on text-only tasks, demonstrating its generalizability.
A dynamic steering ratio mechanism allows MoReS to adapt to tasks of varying complexity, with optimal ratios differing per dataset.
papers.abstract: Jinhe Bi, Yujun Wang, Haokun Chen, Xun Xiao, Artur Hecker, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration. VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: Does Time Have Its Place? Temporal Heads: Where Language Models Recall Time-specific Information
papers.research_question: How do language models internally handle and recall temporally changing facts? Specifically, where within the model architecture does the mechanism for time-specific knowledge reside?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers Temporal Heads, specific attention heads that mediate the recall of time-specific knowledge in LLMs. Ablating these heads degrades temporal fact recall while leaving time-invariant knowledge and general QA performance unaffected, and their activations can be used for temporal knowledge editing.
papers.conclusion: The work systematically uncovers Temporal Heads that selectively mediate time-variant knowledge in LLMs. These heads are causally important for temporal recall, can be activated by both numeric and textual time references, and offer a target for precise temporal knowledge editing without global retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Specific attention heads (Temporal Heads) are identified across multiple models (e.g., a15.h0, a18.h3 in Llama2) that are crucial for recalling time-specific facts.
Ablating Temporal Heads significantly reduces accuracy on temporal knowledge tasks but has minimal impact on time-invariant knowledge and general QA performance.
Temporal Heads are activated not only by numeric time conditions (e.g., 'In 2004') but also by textual aliases (e.g., 'In the year the Summer Olympics were held in Athens'), indicating they encode a broader temporal dimension.
The importance of Temporal Heads varies across different years and knowledge categories, with stronger effects around periods of factual transition.
Temporal knowledge can be edited by selectively adjusting the activation values of these heads, demonstrating their role as a key component for modifying time-sensitive information.
papers.limitation:
Analysis of unstructured temporal QAs like General ChroKnowledge was constrained, as the underlying multiple-choice options typically do not exhibit temporal dependencies.
The circuit analysis method (EAP-IG) did not support models with Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), excluding models like Llama-3-8B-Instruct from the main analysis.
future_direction: Future work should include broader application of the findings for enhancing temporal reasoning to increase practical value.

papers.title: Counterfactual Interventions Reveal the Causal Effect of Relative Clause\n Representations on Agreement Prediction
papers.research_question: When language models process syntactically complex sentences, do they use their representations of syntax in a manner that is consistent with the grammar of the language?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AlterRep, a counterfactual intervention method to test if language models use linguistic features consistently with grammar, and finds that BERT uses relative clause boundary information grammatically and abstractly.
papers.conclusion: AlterRep provides a way to test causal use of linguistic features in models, and shows BERT uses relative clause boundaries grammatically and abstractly.
papers.key_findings:
Only middle layers of BERT causally influence agreement prediction in a manner consistent with English grammar, while all layers encode RC boundary information.
RC boundary representations partially generalize across different RC types, suggesting abstract representation.
Interventions using random subspaces do not yield interpretable changes, indicating specificity of RC subspaces.
Similar patterns observed in BERT variants of different sizes, except BERT-tiny.
papers.limitation: AlterRep uses linear subspaces to analyze non-linear networks, so negative results may not be conclusive.
future_direction: Apply AlterRep to test hypotheses about a wide range of linguistic structures and tasks.
papers.abstract:
When language models process syntactically complex sentences, do they use
their representations of syntax in a manner that is consistent with the grammar
of the language? We propose AlterRep, an intervention-based method to address
this question. For any linguistic feature of a given sentence, AlterRep
generates counterfactual representations by altering how the feature is
encoded, while leaving intact all other aspects of the original representation.
By measuring the change in a model's word prediction behavior when these
counterfactual representations are substituted for the original ones, we can
draw conclusions about the causal effect of the linguistic feature in question
on the model's behavior. We apply this method to study how BERT models of
different sizes process relative clauses (RCs). We find that BERT variants use
RC boundary information during word prediction in a manner that is consistent
with the rules of English grammar; this RC boundary information generalizes to
a considerable extent across different RC types, suggesting that BERT
represents RCs as an abstract linguistic category.

papers.title: Tracing Multilingual Representations in LLMs with Cross-Layer Transcoders
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs form shared representations across languages with language-specific decoding, and why does performance favor the dominant training language such as English?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs form a shared language-agnostic representation space in middle layers, with language-specific decoding in late layers; performance gaps are mechanistically explained by tokenizer bias and feature strength differences.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs use shared representations in middle layers and language-specific decoding in late layers, with performance gaps explained by feature strength and tokenizer bias.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs consistently form a shared language-agnostic space in middle layers, regardless of English dominance in training data.
Language-specific decoding depends on a small set of high-frequency features in late layers that linearly encode language identity from early layers.
Non-English performance failures are linked to dim late-layer features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizer bias forcing early layers to specialize in word reassembly.
Finetuning strengthens these features and their connections, improving token assembly and language-specific decoding.
The shared multilingual space emerges as an architectural property, even when models are trained without English.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) can process many languages, yet how they internally represent this diversity remains unclear. Do they form shared multilingual representations with language-specific decoding, and if so, why does performance favor the dominant training language? To address this, we train models on different multilingual mixtures and analyze their internal mechanisms using Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) and Attribution Graphs. Our results reveal multilingual shared representations: the model employs highly similar features across languages, while language-specific decoding emerges in later layers. Training models without English shows identical multilingual shared space structures. Decoding relies partly on a small set of high-frequency features in the final layers, which linearly encode language identity from early layers. Intervening on these features allows one language to be suppressed and another substituted. Finally, to explain non-English failures, we perform a Model-Diffing experiment: underperformance arises from dim late-layer features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizer bias toward English that forces early layers to specialize in word reassembly. Finetuning strengthens these features and their links, improving token assembly and language-specific decoding, providing a mechanistic explanation for multilingual gaps. Our models and CLTs are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/CausalNLP/multilingual-clts and https://huggingface.co/collections/CausalNLP/multilingual-gpt2-models. Our code is available at: https://github.com/abirharrasse/MultilingualCLTs

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: Counterfactual Divergence Singularity: A Theoretical Model of High-Similarity Instability and Micro-Counterfactual Drift in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the relationship between input similarity and output divergence in large language models under micro-counterfactual perturbations be formalized, and what explains the instability near high similarity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Counterfactual Divergence Singularity (CDS), a theoretical framework that characterizes instability in large language models under micro-counterfactual perturbations, showing that divergence increases sharply as semantic similarity approaches unity.
papers.conclusion: The Counterfactual Divergence Singularity (CDS) captures instability in LLMs under micro-counterfactual perturbations, reframing challenges like hallucination as manifestations of local non-smoothness in semantic manifolds, and suggests new evaluation paradigms are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Divergence exhibits a hyperbolic blow-up as semantic similarity approaches 1.
Semantic curvature increases logarithmically in high-similarity regimes.
Embedding drift is minimal for high-similarity pairs, but divergence is high, indicating a contradiction.
LLM semantic manifolds are locally non-smooth, leading to instability near the identity boundary.
The CDS phenomenon provides a geometric explanation for prompt sensitivity, counterfactual failure, and hallucination.
papers.limitation:
Scale and computational constraints with only 200 micro-counterfactual pairs.
Dependency on a single paraphraser (FLAN-T5-Base).
Dependence on a single embedding model (SBERT MiniLM-L6-v2).
Absence of output-level probability divergence analysis.
Limited to English-language textual inputs.
Interpretational boundaries, not claiming CDS explains all hallucinations.
future_direction: Scaling to larger datasets (e.g., 2,000–20,000 pairs).
Testing with different paraphrasers and embedding models.
Including output-level probability divergence analysis.
Extending to other languages and multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable fluency and contextual sensitivity, yet their behaviour under minimal semantic perturbations remains poorly understood. In particular, near-identical paraphrastic inputs—expected to yield stable and equivalent responses—often produce disproportionately divergent generative behaviour. This paper introduces the <bold>Counterfactual Divergence Singularity (CDS)</bold> , a theoretical and empirical framework that characterizes a previously underexplored instability regime in transformer-based language models. This work formalizes micro-counterfactual perturbations as infinitesimal semantic variations in embedding space and show that, as semantic similarity approaches unity, divergence metrics exhibit a hyperbolic blow-up. Using a controlled experimental pipeline based on FLAN-T5-generated paraphrases and Sentence-BERT semantic embeddings, this paper empirically demonstrate that divergence, curvature, and embedding drift collectively reveal a singular boundary where semantic proximity no longer guarantees behavioural stability. Despite minimal embedding displacement and near-maximal cosine similarity, reciprocal divergence measures increase sharply, exposing a structural nonlinearity in the input–output mapping of LLMs. The results suggest that LLM semantic manifolds are locally non-smooth and that standard embedding-based similarity metrics fail to capture instability near the identity boundary. This phenomenon provides a geometric and mathematical explanation for prompt sensitivity, counterfactual failure, and certain forms of hallucination observed in generative systems. By reframing these behaviours as consequences of latent-space singularities rather than isolated decoding artifacts, this work contributes a novel theoretical lens for evaluating robustness, interpretability, and reliability in large language models.

papers.title: The Hidden Dimensions of LLM Alignment: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Orthogonal Safety Directions
papers.research_question: What is the multi-dimensional structure of safety-aligned behavior in LLMs, and how do orthogonal directions in the safety residual space represent distinct safety features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that safety alignment in LLMs is governed by multiple orthogonal directions in activation space, with a dominant direction for refusal and non-dominant directions for features like hypothetical narrative, and that manipulating these directions can bypass safety.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a multi-dimensional mechanistic understanding of what LLMs learn from safety fine-tuning, revealing that safety behavior is controlled by multiple orthogonal directions, which sheds new light on robust alignment research.
papers.key_findings:
The safety residual space is low-rank linear, with a dominant direction that predicts refusal behavior.
Non-dominant directions in the residual space represent interpretable features such as hypothetical narrative and role-playing.
Non-dominant directions causally influence the dominant direction and the model's refusal behavior.
Removing trigger tokens associated with non-dominant directions can bypass the learned safety alignment, revealing vulnerabilities.
Safety fine-tuning may learn spurious correlations from specific jailbreak patterns, limiting generalization.
papers.limitation:
As data complexity and model size increase, the effective rank of the residual space increases, making interpretation of directions more challenging.
The linearity assumption may not hold perfectly, as directions can flip between layers and extending directions indefinitely degrades generation quality.
future_direction: Analyzing the fine-tuning process in smaller intervals or grouping samples by domain.
Preventing models from learning spurious correlations through targeted interventions in activation space or data augmentation for balanced training.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models' safety-aligned behaviors, such as refusing harmful queries, can be represented by linear directions in activation space. Previous research modeled safety behavior with a single direction, limiting mechanistic understanding to an isolated safety feature. In this work, we discover that safety-aligned behavior is jointly controlled by multi-dimensional directions. Namely, we study the vector space of representation shifts during safety fine-tuning on Llama 3 8B for refusing jailbreaks. By studying orthogonal directions in the space, we first find that a dominant direction governs the model's refusal behavior, while multiple smaller directions represent distinct and interpretable features like hypothetical narrative and role-playing. We then measure how different directions promote or suppress the dominant direction, showing the important role of secondary directions in shaping the model's refusal representation. Finally, we demonstrate that removing certain trigger tokens in harmful queries can mitigate these directions to bypass the learned safety capability, providing new insights on understanding safety alignment vulnerability from a multi-dimensional perspective. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/BMPixel/safety-residual-space.

papers.title: Language Arithmetics: Towards Systematic Language Neuron Identification and Manipulation
papers.research_question: How do language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs control language behavior, and can they be manipulated to steer model outputs across languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces language arithmetics, an additive neuron intervention method, to identify and manipulate language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs, showing that it can steer language generation and improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Our large-scale study demonstrates that language-specific neurons encode meaningful linguistic features that can be identified, analyzed, and manipulated to steer model behavior across languages. By employing a novel additive intervention method, we show that activating these neurons allows for generation language control and improves performance on various multilingual tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization.
Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting linguistic proximity.
Additive language arithmetics outperforms replacement-based methods for language forcing.
Activating target-language neurons improves performance on multilingual tasks like translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI.
Models exhibit internal 'fallback' mechanisms for language selection when dominant language neurons are deactivated.
papers.limitation:
Broader evaluation across more diverse downstream settings is needed.
Quality and fluency of forced outputs across languages, especially low-resource ones, remain underexplored.
Analysis focuses on isolated neurons, overlooking distributed representations and circuits.
Computational constraints limited some experiments to smaller models.
future_direction: Investigate the interactions and dependencies between neurons to understand network-level mechanisms supporting multilingual processing.
More detailed investigation of language fallback dynamics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong multilingual abilities, yet the neural mechanisms behind language-specific processing remain unclear. We analyze language-specific neurons in Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, and Aya-Expanse-8B & 32B across 21 typologically diverse languages, identifying neurons that control language behavior. Using the Language Activation Probability Entropy (LAPE) method, we show that these neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization. Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting internal representations of linguistic proximity. Through language arithmetics, i.e. systematic activation addition and multiplication, we steer models to deactivate unwanted languages and activate desired ones, outperforming simpler replacement approaches. These interventions effectively guide behavior across five multilingual tasks: language forcing, translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI. Manipulation is more successful for high-resource languages, while typological similarity improves effectiveness. We also demonstrate that cross-lingual neuron steering enhances downstream performance and reveal internal "fallback" mechanisms for language selection when neurons are progressively deactivated. Our code is made publicly available at https://github.com/d-gurgurov/Language-Neurons-Manipulation.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: Metaphors are a Source of Cross-Domain Misalignment of Large Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Earlier research has shown that metaphors influence human's decision making, which raises the question of whether metaphors also influence large language models (LLMs)' reasoning pathways, considering their training data contain a large number of metaphors. In this work, we investigate the problem in the scope of the emergent misalignment problem where LLMs can generalize patterns learned from misaligned content in one domain to another domain. We discover a strong causal relationship between metaphors in training data and the misalignment degree of LLMs' reasoning contents. With interventions using metaphors in pre-training, fine-tuning and re-alignment phases, models' cross-domain misalignment degrees change significantly. As we delve deeper into the causes behind this phenomenon, we observe that there is a connection between metaphors and the activation of global and local latent features of large reasoning models. By monitoring these latent features, we design a detector that predict misaligned content with high accuracy.

papers.title: Understanding Large Language Model Behaviors through Interactive Counterfactual Generation and Analysis
papers.research_question: How can interactive counterfactual generation and analysis help users understand and explore the behaviors of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces LLM Analyzer, an interactive visualization system that enables users to explore and understand LLM behaviors through counterfactual analysis, featuring a novel algorithm for generating fluent and semantically meaningful counterfactuals.
papers.conclusion: LLM Analyzer provides an interactive approach to understanding LLM behaviors through counterfactual analysis, emphasizing the importance of involving humans as active participants in the explanation process.
papers.key_findings:
LLM Analyzer is effective in supporting users to understand LLM behaviors, as shown by high usability and usefulness scores in user studies.
The counterfactual generation algorithm produces diverse and grammatically correct counterfactuals across multiple domains, with an average grammaticality rate of 97.2%.
Users can successfully answer explanatory questions such as why, what-if, how to be that, and how to still be using the system's interactive features.
The system integrates feature attributions computed via KernelSHAP with concrete examples to provide a comprehensive view of model behavior.
Expert interviews confirm that LLM Analyzer is valuable for LLM practitioners in assessing model trustworthiness and identifying misalignments.
papers.abstract: Understanding the behavior of large language models (LLMs) is crucial for ensuring their safe and reliable use. However, existing explainable AI (XAI) methods for LLMs primarily rely on word-level explanations, which are often computationally inefficient and misaligned with human reasoning processes. Moreover, these methods often treat explanation as a one-time output, overlooking its inherently interactive and iterative nature.
